title: How do you show a regulator that training works?
description: How to build an evidence chain that shows a regulator your training works: obligation and risk, design, assessment, on the job application, and review.
shortAnswer: To show a regulator that training works, present an evidence chain rather than a completion rate: the obligation and risk the training addresses, how the content and assessment were designed from them, proof that people reached the required standard, evidence they apply it at work, what monitoring found, and what you changed as a result. Regulators rarely prescribe metrics, so the logic connecting each link matters as much as the numbers.
keyTakeaways: Completion rates show that training happened. They do not show that it worked, and regulators increasingly ask about both.

Regulators in several markets ask about effectiveness. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) asks prosecutors to examine how a company measures the effectiveness of its compliance training, and Japan's Financial Services Agency (FSA) expects internal audit to cover the effectiveness of employee AML/CFT training.
Build the case as a chain: obligation, risk, design, learning evidence, application evidence, outcome signals, review and change.
Be honest about limits. Showing what you found, including weaknesses, and what you did about them is more credible than a perfect dashboard.

blocks.text: Most regulators expect training to be suitable for the role and risk, and expect you to monitor whether your arrangements work, but few prescribe how to measure effectiveness. The expectation is framed as outcomes and review, not a specific metric. The examples below, from regulators in several markets and from international medicines manufacturing guidance, show the pattern.

items: **US Department of Justice.** The Criminal Division's [Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs](https://www.justice.gov/media/1160391/dl?inline) (September 2024) asks prosecutors whether a company provides appropriately tailored training and communications, and includes questions on how the company measures the effectiveness of its training. The DOJ stresses that its topics "form neither a checklist nor a formula". See [DOJ compliance program training expectations](/regulations/doj-compliance-program-training-expectations).

**US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).** Its [Quality Systems guidance](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/quality-systems-approach-pharmaceutical-current-good-manufacturing-practice-regulations) for drug manufacturers describes training programs that include evaluation of training effectiveness, with managers verifying that skills are applied. The guidance does not add new requirements to 21 CFR 211.25.

**Japan Financial Services Agency.** The FSA's [AML/CFT Guidelines](https://www.fsa.go.jp/en/news/2026/20260331/01.pdf) (revised March 31, 2026) set required actions on human resource development (section III-5) and expect internal audit to cover the effectiveness of employee training (section III-3(3)). See [Japan FSA AML/CFT guidelines training](/regulations/japan-fsa-aml-cft-guidelines-training).

**Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC).** Its [AML/CTF training guidance](https://www.austrac.gov.au/about-us/amlctf-reform/reforms-guidance/amlctf-program-reform/personnel-due-diligence-and-training-reform/amlctf-training-reform) refers to section 26F(4)(e) of the AML/CTF Act and Rules section 5 to 9(2), and lists expectations including that you monitor the effectiveness of your training and evaluate whether personnel are retaining knowledge from it and applying it appropriately.

**Medicines manufacturing.** The PIC/S Guide to GMP, applied by medicines regulators that participate in the PIC/S scheme, including Japan's, says continuing training "should also be given, and its practical effectiveness should be periodically assessed" ([PE009-16 Part I, clause 2.11](https://www.tga.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-03/pe-009-16-gmp-guide-part-i-basic-requirements-medicinal-products.pdf)).

blocks.text: None of these sources says a particular pass mark, survey score, or evaluation model is required. Avoid telling a regulator that your approach is "what they require" unless you can point to the words.

sections.heading: What does a convincing evidence chain look like?

blocks.text: A convincing chain lets a reviewer follow one obligation from the risk it addresses through to observed behavior, with evidence at every link. The table below is an original framework for assembling it.

sections.heading: How do you build the evidence, step by step?

blocks.text: Build the evidence before anyone asks for it. Each step below produces an artifact a regulator can read.

items: **Pick the obligations that matter most.** Rank by regulatory and harm risk. Output: a short list of priority obligations. Use [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations) if the mapping does not exist.
**Write the effectiveness question for each.** For example: do onboarding staff correctly escalate unusual customer behavior? Output: one question per obligation.

**Choose evidence for each link in the chain.** Prefer evidence the business already produces, such as quality assurance reviews or incident logs. Output: an evidence plan. The measurement design is covered in [how to measure training effectiveness](/guides/how-to-measure-training-effectiveness).
**Set a baseline and a review cadence.** Output: baseline figures and dates for the next reviews.
**Collect and interpret.** Look for patterns by role, team, and content version, and separate training causes from process or system causes. Output: a findings note.
**Act and record.** Change content, assessments, supervision, or procedures, and record why. Output: a change log linked to the findings.
**Summarize for the regulator.** A short narrative per obligation, supported by the artifacts. Output: an effectiveness statement.

sections.heading: What does this look like in practice?

blocks.title: Illustrative example, not a real case
blocks.text: A remittance business retrains its customer onboarding team on revised customer due diligence procedures. The chain it keeps: the AML/CFT risk assessment entry for onboarding; role specific outcomes signed off by the AML/CFT compliance officer; a scenario assessment in which staff must identify missing beneficial ownership information; monthly quality assurance sampling of onboarding files before and after training; the rate of files returned for incomplete checks; and a record that one scenario was rewritten after most staff failed it for reasons traced to an unclear procedure step, which was also fixed.

The strength of this example is not any single number. It is that each claim is backed by a document, the business looked for evidence beyond the classroom, and it recorded what it changed when the evidence pointed to a problem.
The most common weaknesses are relying on completion rates, claiming causation from a single trend, and presenting evidence that was assembled after the question was asked.

items: Reporting 98 percent completion as proof of effectiveness.
Attributing a fall in incidents entirely to training when procedures, staffing, or systems also changed.
Presenting satisfaction scores as evidence of competence.
Hiding negative findings. A regulator who finds them independently will question everything else.
Evidence with no dates or versions, which cannot be tied to the period under review.

blocks.text: The fix for most of these is to move evidence up the chain. Replace completion counts with assessment results tied to outcomes, and add evidence of application such as file reviews or [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency). The [completion tracking versus competency verification](/compare/completion-tracking-vs-competency-verification) comparison sets out the difference in more detail, and [the Kirkpatrick model](/glossary/kirkpatrick-model) gives a common vocabulary for the levels of evidence.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines the obligation, learning outcomes, and assessment points as a connected framework before content is written, and keeps provenance for each. The first links of the evidence chain therefore exist by design, and assessment results can be read against the specific outcomes and obligations they were built to test.

faqs.q: Do regulators require the Kirkpatrick model?
faqs.a: No regulator source reviewed for this guide requires a specific evaluation model. The Kirkpatrick model is a widely used way to structure evidence across reaction, learning, behavior, and results, and it maps well onto an evidence chain, but you should present it as your chosen method, not as a regulatory requirement.

faqs.q: What if we cannot prove training caused an improvement?
faqs.a: Say so. Few organizations can isolate the effect of training from other changes. A credible case shows that the training was designed from the risk, that people reached the standard, that they apply it, and that trends are monitored and acted on. Stating the limits of attribution adds credibility.

faqs.q: How often should effectiveness be reviewed?
faqs.a: Set the cadence by risk and by what the business already reviews. Many organizations align it with their compliance monitoring or program review cycle, and add a review after any significant regulatory change, incident, or content release. Record the cadence in your training policy so you can show it was followed.

faqs.q: Is a survey of staff confidence useful evidence?
faqs.a: It is useful as a leading signal and for spotting unclear content, but it is weak evidence of competence on its own. Pair it with assessment results and evidence of application at work.

factCheck.claim: AUSTRAC expects entities to monitor the effectiveness of training and evaluate whether personnel retain knowledge and apply it appropriately; references Act s26F(4)(e) and Rules s5 to 9(2).

PIC/S GMP Part I clause 2.11: newly recruited personnel should receive training appropriate to the duties assigned to them; continuing training should also be given, and its practical effectiveness should be periodically assessed.

DOJ ECCP section I.C Training and Communications: appropriately tailored training and communications; sample questions on form, content and effectiveness of training; topics 'form neither a checklist nor a formula'; September 2024 version current as at September 2026.

FDA Quality Systems guidance (2006) expects training programs with evaluation of effectiveness and managers verifying skills are applied; references 211.25(a) and (b); does not introduce new requirements.
FSA AML/CFT Guidelines revised and current as of March 31, 2026; III-5 human resource development required actions; III-3(3) audit of effectiveness of employee training.
Japan (MHLW and PMDA) acceded to PIC/S in July 2014.
